common_name: Tennessee Waltz Fuchsia (Semi-Double Lavender-and-Rose Bedding Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Tennessee Waltz is a mid-20th-century American upright bedding fuchsia valued for its heat tolerance relative to most fuchsia hybrids.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun. Tennessee Waltz bears an abundance of semi-double to double flowers with recurved, twisting rose-red sepals surrounding a lavender-blue corolla, on a vigorous, self-branching, upright-bushy plant that needs little pinching to stay full. Bred in the United States and released in 1951, it has remained one of the most widely grown American fuchsias because it holds up to heat and sun noticeably better than most fuchsia hybrids, making it one of the more forgiving choices for Gulf Coast patios and hanging baskets as long as soil stays consistently moist. Pinch young plants once or twice to encourage branching, and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain continuous bloom from late spring into fall.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; Checkerboard was bred in California from Fuchsia magellanica stock and is more sun- and heat-tolerant than typical hybrid-bell fuchsias.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, tolerating a bit more sun than most hybrid fuchsias once established. Checkerboard produces slender, elongated, unskirted flowers rather than the typical flared bell shape, with a long tube that is red at the base and white toward the tip, giving each pendant bloom a distinctive two-toned, checkerboard-like banding, set off by red sepals and a small purple corolla. Bred by Victor Reiter Jr. of San Francisco from Fuchsia magellanica lineage, it grows into a vigorous, upright, branching shrub that is often used for informal hedges or screening in mild-summer climates. In the humid Gulf South it appreciates afternoon shade and a thick mulch layer, dying back hard in a freeze but often resprouting from the base where winters stay above the low teens.

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Snowcap is a Victorian-era English cultivar still grown for its prolific, weather-resistant flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, out of hot afternoon sun. Snowcap bears masses of small-to-medium semi-double flowers with pure white sepals over a cherry-red to cerise corolla, on a dense, compact, self-branching upright bush that flowers with exceptional freedom from late spring through fall. Raised in England in the 1880s, it remains a mainstay of fuchsia bedding displays and trained standards because the flowers are weather-tolerant and the plant needs minimal pinching to stay full. In hot, humid Gulf Coast summers it slows its bloom during peak heat, so give it reliable afternoon shade, consistent moisture, and regular feeding to keep it flowering into the cooler shoulder seasons.

common_name: La Campanella Fuchsia (Semi-Double White-and-Purple Trailing Basket Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; La Campanella is a naturally trailing Austrian-bred fuchsia grown extensively for hanging baskets.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun. La Campanella smothers itself in small, semi-double flowers with blush-white sepals tinged rose and an imperial-purple corolla that fades to lavender with age, carried on naturally lax, trailing stems that need little to no pinching to cascade over a basket's rim. Bred in Austria in 1968, it is among the most widely grown basket fuchsias worldwide because of its self-branching habit and nonstop flower production. It blooms most heavily in cool, humid conditions and stalls in peak summer heat, so Gulf Coast growers should site baskets in bright shade with steady moisture and regular feeding to carry bloom through the hottest months.

common_name: Nellie Nuttall Fuchsia (Compact Single Red-and-White Exhibition Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Nellie Nuttall is a compact English exhibition fuchsia prized for flowers that hold their shape and color in poor weather.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, out of hot afternoon sun. Nellie Nuttall carries neat, well-formed single flowers with bright red sepals held crisply above a white, red-veined corolla, on a compact, upright, naturally bushy plant that needs only light pinching. Raised in England in 1977, it became a favorite among fuchsia show growers because the small, precisely shaped flowers resist rain damage and fading better than most cultivars, staying tidy for containers and borders alike. In humid Gulf Coast summers it benefits from steady afternoon shade and consistent moisture; expect flowering to ease during the hottest weeks and pick back up as temperatures moderate in fall.

common_name: Phyllis Fuchsia (Vigorous Sun-Tolerant Rose-Red Hedging Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; Phyllis is an unusually vigorous, sun-tolerant English cultivar from 1938 often grown as an informal hedge or trained standard.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade, though established plants tolerate more direct sun than most fuchsias provided the soil stays evenly moist. Phyllis produces abundant small-to-medium semi-double flowers, both sepals and corolla a self rose-red, on an exceptionally vigorous, upright, woody-based bush that can be grown as a loose informal hedge, trained as a standard, or cut back hard each year as a large border perennial. Raised in England in 1938, it is valued for shrugging off wind, rain, and heat better than more delicate hybrids. In the Gulf South it behaves as a half-hardy perennial, dying back to the base in a hard freeze but often resprouting where winters stay above the mid-teens, and it flowers most heavily once summer heat begins to ease.

common_name: Empress of Prussia Fuchsia (Heritage Single Scarlet Self-Colored Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; Empress of Prussia is an 1868 English heritage cultivar valued for its vigor and relative hardiness among hybrid fuchsias.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade. Empress of Prussia bears an abundance of single, self-colored scarlet-cerise flowers, sepals and corolla nearly matching in hue, on a strong, upright, bushy plant that begins flowering earlier in the season and continues later than many hybrids. Raised in England in 1868, it is counted among the hardier heritage fuchsias and is often grown as a border or low-hedge perennial in climates too cold for tender bedding types, dying back to the ground in freezing weather and resprouting from the roots in spring. In the Gulf South, give it afternoon shade and a heavy winter mulch over the crown; it rewards Gulf Coast growers with strong summer heat tolerance for a hybrid fuchsia and continues blooming well into fall.

common_name: Celia Smedley Fuchsia (Large Single Pink-and-Ruby Exhibition Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Celia Smedley is a vigorous English exhibition cultivar from 1970 often trained as a standard.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, out of hot afternoon sun. Celia Smedley bears unusually large single flowers with pale pink sepals held above a ruby-red to carmine corolla, on a strong, vigorous, upright plant that responds well to training as a standard or large patio specimen. Raised in England in 1970, it has won repeated show awards and is considered one of the finest exhibition fuchsias for the size and substance of its blooms. In humid Gulf Coast conditions it wants steady afternoon shade and consistent moisture to keep its large flowers from stressing in the heat; feed regularly and expect the heaviest bloom during the cooler shoulder-season months.

common_name: Border Queen Fuchsia (Compact Pale Pink-and-Lilac Bedding Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Border Queen is a compact English bedding cultivar from 1974 noted for weather-resistant flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade. Border Queen carries dainty single-to-semi-double flowers with pale pink sepals over a pale lavender-mauve corolla veined pink at the base, on a compact, neat, well-branched bush that needs little pinching to stay tidy in beds and containers. Raised in England in 1974, it is prized for holding its bloom color and shape well through wind and rain compared to many pastel cultivars. In the Gulf South, give it reliable afternoon shade and steady moisture; it tends to slow during the hottest weeks of summer and resumes heavy flowering as temperatures ease into fall.

common_name: Ting-a-Ling Fuchsia (Pure White Single-Flowered Upright Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Ting-a-Ling is an American-bred cultivar from 1959 valued as one of the few true all-white fuchsias.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, out of hot afternoon sun. Ting-a-Ling produces single, waxy, pure white flowers with only the faintest pink blush at the tube, both sepals and corolla white, on a sturdy, upright, self-branching bush; the all-white coloring is unusual among fuchsias and makes it a favorite for pairing with brighter red and purple cultivars. Bred in the United States in 1959, it remains a widely grown American variety for beds, containers, and mixed plantings. In Gulf Coast gardens the pale flowers can show heat stress in peak summer, so keep it in steady afternoon shade with consistent moisture, and expect the cleanest white blooms during the cooler spring and fall months.

common_name: Coachman Fuchsia (Self-Colored Orange-Salmon Trailing Basket Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in partial shade in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or container mix; Coachman is an English cultivar grown for its unusual self-colored orange-salmon flowers and naturally trailing habit.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil or container mix in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun. Coachman bears single, self-colored salmon-orange flowers, sepals and corolla nearly matching in hue, an unusual solid warm color among fuchsias that are more typically bicolor red-and-purple, carried on naturally lax, trailing stems well suited to hanging baskets. It flowers most freely in cool, humid weather and needs only light pinching to encourage a full basket shape. In the Gulf South it slows noticeably during the hottest summer weeks, so site baskets in bright shade with steady moisture and regular feeding to sustain bloom into fall.

common_name: Swanley Gem Fuchsia (Heirloom Vigorous Scarlet-and-Purple Bedding Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; Swanley Gem is an English heirloom cultivar from 1901 valued for its vigor and free branching habit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade. Swanley Gem produces single flowers with scarlet-red sepals over a rich purple corolla that ages to reddish-purple, on a vigorous, freely branching, upright-bushy plant that fills out quickly without much pinching. Raised in England in 1901, this heirloom cultivar has remained popular for bedding and low hedging because of its reliable, weather-tolerant flower production over a long season. In the Gulf South it behaves as a half-hardy perennial, cut back by hard freezes but often returning from the base where winters stay mild, and it holds up to summer heat and humidity better than many newer, more delicate hybrids provided it gets afternoon shade and consistent moisture.
